expectations.text: A representative runnable example of the typical call pattern is present and follows the audience rules
expectations.evidence: Example_throttle has an // Output: block and passes (go test -run Example verified in the -v run). It demonstrates the mandated Allow-then-Wait-on-false pattern with defer Close. Doc comment addresses users about the scenario ('A bursty client is the typical caller...'); in-function comments explain the non-obvious New(2, 2) inputs, the defer-Close discipline, the starts-full contract, and Close idempotence at the call sites.

expectations.text: Invalid-input coverage includes the zero-interval boundary: a rate large enough that the refill interval truncates to zero is exercised alongside the documented panic cases
expectations.evidence: The zero-interval case exists only as a commented-out table entry (limiter_test.go lines 151-156: `// {rate: 2_000_000_000, burst: 1, ...}`), so it is never executed: go test -v runs only the zero-rate, negative-rate, and negative-burst cases. The run's stated reason is sound (time.NewTicker(0) panics on the background refill goroutine, an unrecoverable process crash mustPanic cannot catch, and report.md frames it as contract drift needing an author decision), and the corpus blesses comment-out to see work through, but its hand-off rule is to restore the case, and report.md explicitly rejects restoring it. As shipped, the boundary is documented, not exercised.

expectations.text: Comment discipline: NON-TRIVIAL tests carry a rationale doc comment in layman's terms; trivial ones may carry none; no comment opens with its own function name; no comment explains conventions, test ordering, synctest mechanics, or says a test 'pins the contract' (anti-slop)
expectations.evidence: Both non-trivial tests carry layman rationale doc comments ('The typical client story end to end...', 'A zero-burst limiter holds no reserve...'); the trivial panic table carries none. No test/example doc comment opens with its own function name (mustPanic's does, but it is a plain helper where standard Go doc convention requires the name; the corpus rule targets test/bench/fuzz/example functions only). grep finds no comment about ordering, conventions, synctest mechanics, or 'pins the contract'; the withheld-case comment gives only the technical crash reason and the prose-drift framing.

expectations.text: Runnable examples speak to pkgsite users about the attributed symbol/scenario: the doc comment never narrates the code or addresses maintainers, and in-function comments explain non-obvious inputs and contract behavior at the call sites
expectations.evidence: Example_throttle's doc comment describes the throttle scenario from the caller's seat without narrating statements or mentioning tests/maintainers. In-function comments do call-site contract work: 'Two tokens per second, and up to two held for a burst' on New(2, 2); 'Always defer Close so the refill goroutine is released...'; 'The limiter starts full, so the opening burst is admitted at once'; 'Closing again is safe: Close is idempotent...' on the second Close.
